# F03 — Elasticity and practice

Original synthetic lecture/practice material, version 1. No official solutions are supplied; any expanded answers are authored.

## Slide 1 — Point elasticity

Define signed own-price point elasticity (partial x / partial px)*(px/x), stating which variables are held fixed. Explain conversion from a unit-dependent slope to a dimensionless relative response. For xy preferences derive ordinary elasticity -1 and compensated elasticity -1/2. Keep income fixed in the first derivative and target utility fixed in the second; they are different experiments.

## Slide 2 — Finite price change

For ordinary demand x=M/(2px), doubling px halves quantity. For compensated demand at fixed positive utility, doubling px multiplies hx by 1/sqrt(2). Explain why a local point elasticity is not a rule to multiply an arbitrary finite percentage change. State the signed and absolute-value conventions; no arc-elasticity calculation is required here.

## Slide 3 — P1: Budget and a boundary case

(a) For u=xy, M=48,px=3,py=2, derive the optimal quantities and check spending. (b) Derive the MRS at this point and compare with the price ratio. (c) Keeping prices/income the same but changing utility to u=x+y, find the choice and justify why the method changes.

## Slide 4 — P2: A full decomposition

For u=xy, M=30,px=py=1 initially, raise px to 9. (a) Find A, B and C, defining each experiment. (b) Find the two x effects and check the total. (c) Compare the Hicks compensation with the extra money needed to buy the old bundle. (d) Write the three budget-line equations and explain their slopes and vertical intercepts. All four subparts matter.

## Slide 5 — P3: Elasticity and a large change

For xy preferences, (a) derive the own-price elasticities of ordinary and compensated x demand and specify the fixed variables; (b) if px triples, find the exact proportional change in each demand; (c) explain why the two changes differ without saying that utility and income are held fixed at once.
